task: Horizon 11 of the agent-agnostic-browser-bridge project (tools/chrome-bridge/). Add a single new generic page action `waitFor` that blocks until a page condition holds before returning: a CSS selector appears in the sandbox tab's DOM, the page's captured network activity goes idle, or a fixed delay elapses — each bounded by a timeout. It targets the dedicated sandbox tab like every other page action, must be CSP-safe (no string eval), and must add no new manifest permission. Resolves package blocker #3. Follow the established add-one-atomic-page-action-across-the-parity-surface then live-Chrome head-to-head verification pattern used by horizons 7-10.

analysis.objective: Add a single atomic generic page action `waitFor` to the chrome-bridge package that blocks until one of three page conditions holds — a CSS selector is present in the sandbox tab's DOM, the tab's captured network activity goes quiet, or a fixed delay elapses — each bounded by a caller-set timeout, shipped across the full parity surface and verified live in Chrome, resolving package blocker #3.
analysis.successDefinition: Done means: (1) `waitFor` is the 20th entry in `PAGE_ACTIONS` with dedicated Params/Result interfaces, both `Record<PageAction, …>` mapped types (extension handler map + MCP tool catalog) updated so tsc stays green, raw + guarded handler entries, a `TOOL_CATALOG` entry with an honest JSON schema for the three mutually-exclusive modes plus `timeoutMs`, both hardcoded action-count assertions bumped, and README count/enumeration/prose/manual-e2e-step all updated; (2) unit tests cover all three modes including the timeout-elapsed path and malformed params, and `npm run verify` (or its reliably-green subset per CLAUDE.md) passes; (3) a live-Chrome head-to-head in a fresh post-rebuild MCP session demonstrates: selector mode returns `met` once a JS-inserted node appears and returns a clean not-met result when the timeout elapses, network-idle mode returns after captured fetch/XHR traffic stops, delay mode blocks for approximately the requested milliseconds, every mode is capped by its timeout, the manifest diff adds no new permission, and no caller-supplied string is evaluated as JavaScript.
assumptions: `waitFor` is a new standalone page action (PAGE_ACTIONS 19→20), NOT a `{waitFor, timeoutMs}` option retrofitted onto `readPage`/`getPageText`/`scrollPage` as blocker #3's original wording suggested — the horizon 7-10 pattern is one atomic action across the parity surface.

The action takes one required mode discriminator resolving to exactly three shapes (selector-present, network-idle, fixed-delay) plus a `timeoutMs` with a sane default and a hard upper cap kept below the MCP command timeout.
The Result reports which condition was checked, whether it was satisfied or the timeout was hit, and elapsed milliseconds; a timeout is a normal `{ met: false }` result, not a thrown error.

Selector polling runs CSP-safe through `chrome.scripting.executeScript` with a function reference in the ISOLATED world (the mechanism `findElement` already uses); the h8 ban is only on caller-supplied string eval.

Network-idle is derived from the existing per-tab network ring buffer (a quiet window with no new captured entries), because that capture already exists and adds no permission; a CDP `Network` domain subscription is a fallback only if the ring buffer proves insufficient.
The action targets the dedicated sandbox tab via the existing tab-resolution path like every other page action, and retains per-command `chrome.debugger` attach/detach — no persistent CDP session.
`chrome.scripting` and `chrome.debugger` are already granted, so the no-new-permission constraint is satisfiable by construction.
Fixed-delay mode is implemented with a timer in the service-worker handler / poll module, not page-side code.
Long-deferred housekeeping (deleting the dead active-tab surface, fixing stale count comments) is folded in only if it stays a few lines; it is not a horizon goal.

All binding decisions in decisions.md (CDP scope, sandbox-tab-only targeting, `as const` literals, Claude-Code-only verification, manual-Chrome check to close the horizon) remain in force and are not re-litigated.
risks: Selector polling in the deliberately-unfocused sandbox tab cannot observe IntersectionObserver-gated / `content-visibility` / lazy-rendered nodes (h10 discovery: render pass suspended), so `waitFor` selector may time out on exactly the virtualized content it is meant to de-flake — the honest scope is JS-driven DOM mutation only, and the tool doc must say so.

Network-idle detection may be unreliable or ill-defined: choosing the idle signal source (ring-buffer quiescence vs CDP `Network` events), the quiet-window duration, and how sub-resource/streaming/websocket traffic counts is a real design decision that can slip.
The live-Chrome head-to-head needs a deterministic public test page that both inserts a DOM node on a timer and fires a delayed network request; without one the verification is hand-wavy.
Repeating the horizon 9 failure mode — the mandatory live check blocked because the MCP session was stale and the new action was not callable; the plan mandates a fresh post-rebuild MCP session.

Misreading the 'no string eval' constraint and either over-restricting (avoiding CDP `Runtime.evaluate` with fixed internal expressions, which is already permitted) or under-restricting (accepting a caller-supplied predicate string).
Parity-surface drift: the count comments, README enumeration, and two hardcoded count tests are easy to miss one of, and the stale count comments already show this class of miss recurring.
outOfScope: Trusted keyboard input via CDP `Input.dispatchKeyEvent` — a separate horizon-11 candidate the user did not pick; one capability per horizon.
Trusted click-by-coordinate via CDP `Input.dispatchMouseEvent` press/release — another candidate not chosen; synthetic `clickAt`/`hover` stay as-is.
`findElement` returning element refs/text/attributes (blocker #6) — distinct extraction slice; `waitFor` only needs an existence check, not a payload.
Capturing network response bodies for RSC/octet-stream responses (blocker #4) — orthogonal capture-layer work; network-idle only needs request timing, not bodies.
`clickElement` by text / XPath and a fuller event sequence (blocker #5) — separate interaction slice, unrelated to waiting.
Full-page / element screenshots, `captureTab({fullPage:true})` (blocker #7) — independent capture feature.
Reviving horizon 5's DOM page-model / bbox snapshot action — explicitly a different deferred capability; not a wait primitive.
A `waitForNavigation` mode — only three modes are in scope (selector, network-idle, fixed delay); navigation settling is a future addition.

Embedding an automatic settle/`waitFor` option inside `readPage`, `getPageText`, `scrollPage` or other existing actions — this horizon ships one standalone action; retrofitting other actions' params is a later, larger change.
Introducing a persistent multi-command CDP session — per-command attach/detach is retained; waiting does not force otherwise.
Making virtualized/lazy list rows materialize in the unfocused sandbox tab — the h10 render-pass-suspension limit is unchanged; `waitFor` observes JS-driven mutation, it does not fix rendering.
Migrating boky's extension / relay / MCP onto the new tool — the whole project is reuse-extraction, never a boky refactor (binding decision).
analysis.domainShapeReason: The task is about browser-automation machinery — a CDP/`chrome.scripting`-driven page-action added across a typed parity surface in an MV3 extension bridge — with no business entities, rules, or workflows involved.

ubiquitousLanguage.meaning: one generic verb the bridge exposes (e.g. `readPage`, `scrollPage`); `waitFor` becomes the 20th, defined once in the `PAGE_ACTIONS` tuple.

the fixed set of places a new action must be added together — `PAGE_ACTIONS`, Params/Result interfaces, the extension handler map and the MCP `TOOL_CATALOG` (both typed `Record<PageAction, …>`), the two hardcoded count tests, and the README — kept in lockstep by tsc.
the dedicated, deliberately-unfocused Chrome tab that every page action targets; its browser render pass is suspended while JS execution and DOM mutation continue.
which of the three conditions a `waitFor` call blocks on: selector-present, network-idle, or fixed-delay — mutually exclusive in the params.
the caller-set `timeoutMs` (with a default and a hard cap below the MCP command timeout) that bounds every wait mode; hitting it yields a not-met result, not an error.
a quiet window during which no new fetch/XHR entries land in the tab's existing per-tab network ring buffer.
letting the page reach a stable state before a read; the gap `waitFor` fills so verification no longer needs hand-inserted delays between actions.
one `chrome.debugger` attach → command → detach cycle via `withDebuggerSession`; kept per-command, not persistent.
the mandatory horizon-closing check run through the chrome-bridge MCP in a fresh post-rebuild session against real pages, comparing the new action's behavior across its modes.

discoveryFindings.finding: page-actions.ts findElement handler: validates non-empty selector, `await sandboxTab.resolveTabId()`, then `ports.executeScript(tabId, (selector) => { try { return document.querySelectorAll(selector).length } catch { return 0 } }, [params.selector])` — ISOLATED world, function reference, args array carries the selector. It must own its own setTimeout/poll-interval loop with a hard timeoutMs cap and ALWAYS resolve to `{result:{met:false,...}}` on timeout (never throw). phases.name: Add wait-condition poll module
phases.goal: Create a standalone module that repeatedly checks one of three page conditions (a CSS selector is present, captured network traffic has gone quiet, or a fixed delay elapsed) and resolves with a met/not-met outcome once the condition holds or a caller-set timeout budget is spent.
phases.rationale: The chrome-bridge package currently has no handler that polls over time — every existing page action does a single one-shot check and returns. A time-bounded polling loop with a hard timeout cap is the only genuinely new logic in this feature, so it is built and unit-tested in isolation with simulated (fake) timers before it is connected to anything user-facing.
changes: Create wait-condition.ts exporting one async function that takes a mode descriptor (selector-present | network-idle | fixed-delay), a timeoutMs, and injected check callbacks, and returns `{ mode, met, elapsedMs }`.

Implement a poll loop with a fixed interval and a hard timeout cap kept well below the 30s end-to-end command ceiling (default ~10-15s, hard cap ~25s); on timeout resolve `{ met: false }` — never throw.

Selector mode calls a passed-in existence check (count > 0); network-idle mode calls a passed-in 'latest network seq / timestamp' probe and treats 'no new entries for a quiet window' as met, re-arming the window when a new entry arrives; fixed-delay mode simply waits then resolves met.

Add wait-condition.unit.test.ts using vi.useFakeTimers()/vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync covering: selector appears mid-poll, selector never appears (timeout path), network goes quiet, network never quiets (timeout path), fixed delay elapses, and a rejected/invalid timeoutMs.
inputs: discovery finding 'Async/delay/polling precedent in handlers' — no existing poll loop; must own its setTimeout loop and always resolve on timeout
discovery finding 'MCP / relay command timeout' — 30s hard end-to-end ceiling
discovery finding 'Test helpers & fake-timer availability' — vi.useFakeTimers usable, not yet used in page-actions tests
src/extension/capture-store.ts readNetwork shape (`{ entries, nextSince }`, monotonic seq)
phases.expectedResult: tools/chrome-bridge/src/extension/wait-condition.ts exists with passing wait-condition.unit.test.ts exercising all three wait modes plus each timeout-budget path.

rubric.label: Timeout budget always resolves to a not-met outcome
rubric.ruleStatement: For every mode, when the condition never holds, the exported function must resolve to `{ mode, met: false, elapsedMs }` within the hard cap and must never reject, throw, or hang. Scale: 10 = timeout path resolves cleanly for all three modes AND for a check callback that itself throws/rejects (error swallowed into met:false or handled, not propagated) AND elapsedMs is bounded by the hard cap; 8 = all three modes resolve met:false on timeout with a fake-timer test each; minScore 7 = at least selector and network-idle timeout paths resolve met:false and no code path has an uncaught throw on the timeout branch.
passCriteria: Run `pnpm vitest run src/extension/wait-condition.unit.test.ts` — tests named for 'selector never appears', 'network never quiets' (or equivalents) exist and assert the resolved value is `{ met: false }`, not a rejection
Grep the source: the timeout branch calls `resolve(...)` and there is no `throw` / `reject(` reachable from the poll loop's timeout handling
Add a throwing check callback (or inspect an existing test) — the function still resolves, does not surface the error to the caller
Inspect that the loop has an absolute deadline (injected clock / Date.now() compared to `min(timeoutMs, HARD_CAP)`) so a slow/never-returning condition cannot exceed the cap
failureExamples: Poll loop uses `setInterval` + a separate `setTimeout` for the deadline but the interval callback `await`s an async selector check that rejects; the rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection instead of resolving met:false — tests pass because they only use synchronous check stubs

Function resolves met:false on timeout but computes `elapsedMs` from loop counter × interval, so a check callback taking 400ms each iteration lets total elapsed drift well past the hard cap before the deadline is noticed
fixed-delay mode is `setTimeout(resolve, timeoutMs)` with no clamp, so a caller passing 60000 waits past the 30s command timeout

rubric.label: Poll interval fixed and timeout budget clamped below the command ceiling
rubric.ruleStatement: The poll interval must be a fixed bounded constant and the effective budget must be `clamp(timeoutMs ?? DEFAULT, floor, HARD_CAP)` with HARD_CAP well below 30s (default ~10-15s, cap ~25s). Scale: 10 = named constants for interval, default, floor, and hard cap; invalid/absent/negative/NaN/huge timeoutMs each provably clamped by a test; interval never busy-loops (>= ~50ms); 8 = default and hard cap applied and one 'invalid timeoutMs' test; minScore 7 = timeoutMs above cap is clamped to the cap and a missing timeoutMs uses the default, both observable in tests.
passCriteria: Source defines named constants (e.g. `POLL_INTERVAL_MS`, `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS`, `HARD_CAP_MS`) with HARD_CAP_MS <= 25000 and DEFAULT within ~10000-15000

Unit test 'invalid timeoutMs' passes 0 / negative / NaN / undefined / 999999 and asserts the resolved `elapsedMs` (under fake timers) or an exposed effective-budget is the clamped value, not the raw input
The interval between checks is a constant, not derived from `timeoutMs` and not 0; no `setInterval(fn, 0)` / `while(true)` without an await+delay
No `any`, no `!`, no bumped test timeouts (`pnpm lint` + coverage guard green for the two files)
failureExamples: Dev clamps the upper bound to HARD_CAP but leaves the lower bound open, so `timeoutMs: 0` or `-5` makes the loop resolve met:false on the first tick — a caller typo silently disables the wait instead of being floored

`timeoutMs` is passed straight through with only `timeoutMs ?? DEFAULT`; a caller value of 40000 is honored and the surrounding 30s command timeout fires first, so the action returns a transport error instead of a clean not-met result
Poll interval is `timeoutMs / 100`, which for a 200ms fixed-delay caller becomes a 2ms busy loop

rubric.label: All three wait modes implemented with correct met semantics
rubric.ruleStatement: selector-present resolves met:true only when the injected existence check reports count>0; network-idle resolves met:true only after a quiet window with no new network seq/timestamp advance; fixed-delay resolves met:true after the delay regardless of page state. Modes are mutually exclusive via a discriminated descriptor. Scale: 10 = each mode has a 'condition becomes true mid-poll' test AND network-idle correctly re-arms its quiet window when a new entry arrives during the wait; 8 = all three happy-path tests plus selector/network timeout tests present and green; minScore 7 = each mode's happy path is tested and network-idle actually compares two samples over time rather than trusting a single probe.
passCriteria: Tests exist and pass for: 'selector appears mid-poll', 'network goes quiet', 'fixed delay elapses' — each asserting `met: true` and a plausible `elapsedMs`
network-idle test advances fake timers, injects a new network seq partway through the quiet window, and asserts the function does NOT resolve met:true until a full quiet window passes with no advance
The mode descriptor is a discriminated union; passing an unknown kind is a compile error or a rejected/handled input, not a silent fixed-delay
fixed-delay path does not call the selector or network probe at all (test spy asserts zero calls)
failureExamples: network-idle samples the latest network seq once at loop start, then compares against that frozen baseline; any request before the wait makes it never idle, and if none did it reports idle immediately even while requests fire — happy-path test with a static buffer still passes

selector-present resolves met:true on a truthy-ish check of the returned object instead of `count > 0`, so it always resolves immediately on the first poll; the 'appears mid-poll' test passes because the selector is present by tick 2 anyway
fixed-delay is routed through the same poll loop and only resolves on a tick boundary, so a 100ms delay with a 250ms interval waits 250ms; the test asserts `>= 100` so it doesn't catch the drift

rubric.label: Module is standalone with injected checks and controllable clock
rubric.ruleStatement: wait-condition.ts imports no `chrome.*`, no DOM globals, no sibling extension modules, and no real wall-clock/timer the test cannot control; selector existence, network probe, delay, and time source are all parameters or standard timers vi.useFakeTimers patches. Scale: 10 = zero imports from `./` peers, time via an injected `now()` or vi-patchable timers, unit test uses fake timers with no real `await sleep`; 8 = no chrome/DOM refs and checks injected but the module reaches for `Date.now()` directly (still fake-timer-controllable); minScore 7 = no `chrome.*` / `document` / `window` references and the named callbacks are injected rather than imported.
passCriteria: `grep -nE 'chrome\.|document\.|window\.|navigator\.' src/extension/wait-condition.ts` returns nothing
`grep -nE "from '\\./" src/extension/wait-condition.ts` returns nothing (or only type-only imports from `types.ts`)
The exported function signature takes the mode descriptor, timeoutMs, and callback(s) as arguments — verified by reading the signature
The unit test file contains `vi.useFakeTimers()` and `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync`, no real-time `setTimeout`/`sleep` awaits, and no bumped `testTimeout`
Dead-export scanner and coverage guard pass: the single export is referenced in the test, tests are `.unit.test.ts` siblings
failureExamples: Module injects the checks but calls `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, POLL_INTERVAL_MS))` on the real timer; the dev writes the test with `vi.useFakeTimers()` but the promise chain never flushes, so they quietly raise the test timeout to 30000 to make it green

network-idle probe is injected, but the module also imports the network ring-buffer type AND a `getNetworkBuffer()` helper from a sibling file 'just for the default', coupling the pure module to infrastructure
Time is read via `performance.now()` which vi fake timers do not patch by default, so elapsedMs in tests is always ~0 and the timeout-path tests can't advance to the deadline

rubric.label: Returned outcome shape is exact and elapsedMs is truthful
rubric.ruleStatement: Every resolution returns exactly `{ mode, met, elapsedMs }` with `mode` echoing the input kind, `met` a boolean, `elapsedMs` a non-negative integer within `0 <= elapsedMs <= effectiveBudget` (and >= the delay for a completed fixed-delay). No extra/missing keys. Scale: 10 = shape asserted field-by-field in every test, elapsedMs monotonic and bounded, a met:true mid-poll case asserts elapsedMs strictly between one interval and the cap; 8 = shape asserted in happy + timeout tests and elapsedMs bounded; minScore 7 = all resolutions include the three keys with correct types and elapsedMs is never negative or NaN.
passCriteria: Read every `resolve(...)` call site — all produce an object literal with exactly `mode`, `met`, `elapsedMs`
At least one test asserts the full object with `toEqual({ mode: 'network-idle', met: true, elapsedMs: <number> })` rather than only `result.met`
Timeout tests assert `elapsedMs` is approximately the effective budget (within one poll interval), proving it's measured not hard-coded
fixed-delay test asserts `elapsedMs >= delayMs`
No `elapsedMs` value in any test is `NaN`, negative, or a non-integer float from unrounded division
failureExamples: `elapsedMs` is the clamped budget on the timeout path and `Date.now() - start` on the success path; the dev hard-codes the timeout value as `HARD_CAP_MS` so a test clamping to a 5s custom budget still sees `elapsedMs: 25000`

Return object spreads the input descriptor (`{ ...mode, met, elapsedMs }`) so a selector-present result carries an extra `selector` field; the test uses `toMatchObject` so it never catches the leak, and a downstream zod schema later rejects it
fixed-delay resolves with `elapsedMs: 0` because elapsed is captured before the `await delay` rather than after

phases.healerHint: The most likely failure is the network-idle mode trusting a single point-in-time probe instead of re-sampling the network seq/timestamp across the quiet window and re-arming when a new entry appears — fix it to require two consecutive samples spanning at least `quietMs` with no advance before resolving met:true.

phases.name: Add waitFor page action across parity surface
phases.goal: Add `waitFor` as the 20th page action across the fixed lockstep set of files (action tuple, protocol types, extension handler maps, MCP tool catalog, count assertions, README), with its handler validating params and delegating to the wait-condition poll module.
phases.rationale: A new bridge action is only usable when it is registered in every place the codebase keeps in sync: the master list of actions, the request/response type maps, the service-worker handler table, the MCP tool schema advertised to clients, the hardcoded action-count tests, and the README. Missing any one of these breaks the build or ships an inconsistent tool. This mirrors exactly how the recent scrollPage, evaluatePage, and getTabState actions were each added.
changes: Append `waitFor` to the PAGE_ACTIONS `as const` tuple in actions.ts (19 -> 20 entries).

In types.ts add WaitForParams (mode discriminator resolving to selector-present | network-idle | fixed-delay, plus optional timeoutMs) and WaitForResult (`{ mode, met, elapsedMs }`, all readonly primitives), and add one key to each of PageActionParams and PageActionResults.

In page-actions.ts add a `resolveWaitForParams`-style validator that rejects a malformed mode / out-of-range timeoutMs before any tab is resolved, then a raw handler entry that resolves the sandbox tab and calls the wait-condition module (selector check via ports.executeScript with the findElement injected-function shape; network-idle via captureStore.readNetwork using the returned nextSince cursor; fixed-delay via the module's timer), plus the matching guarded entry.

In tool-catalog.ts add a WAIT_FOR_PROPERTIES `as const` block (SCROLL_PROPERTIES precedent) encoding the three mutually-exclusive modes and timeoutMs honestly with `additionalProperties: false`, and add the TOOL_CATALOG entry; the tool description scopes selector mode to JS-driven DOM mutation (not IntersectionObserver / content-visibility / lazy-rendered nodes).

Bump the two hardcoded action-count assertions (actions.unit.test.ts toBe(19)->20 and its ordered-tuple array; tool-catalog.unit.test.ts nineteen/19->twenty/20) and add a `pageActionHandlers — waitFor` describe block covering the three modes and the timeout-elapsed not-met result using fake timers; update README count word, both service-worker/tool enumerations, the '19 tools' manual-e2e line, a new manual-e2e step, and a new per-action prose paragraph.
inputs: discovery findings on the parity surface (PAGE_ACTIONS tuple, protocol types 4 edits, double handler map, tool catalog schema block + entry)
discovery finding 'findElement selector-existence mechanism' — exact injected-function shape to reuse
discovery findings 'Hardcoded action-count assertions' and 'README hardcoded action-count / list / e2e spots'
phases.expectedResult: `npm run verify` reliably-green subset passes with `waitFor` present as the 20th entry in PAGE_ACTIONS, its tool-catalog entry, its handler unit tests, and all count/README updates in place.

rubric.label: All lockstep parity sites updated for waitFor
rubric.ruleStatement: Counts every place the parity surface requires waitFor and scores the fraction present and correct: 10 = every site updated plus tsc proves the two `Record<PageAction,…>` maps are exhaustive with no stragglers and no @ts-expect-error/casts hiding a gap; 8 = all functional sites (PAGE_ACTIONS tuple, WaitForParams/WaitForResult, PageActionParams + PageActionResults keys, extension raw+guarded handler entries, MCP TOOL_CATALOG entry) present and typechecking; minScore 7 = every code site present and green even if one is stylistically off; below 7 = any handler map, catalog entry, or params/results key missing.
passCriteria: `grep -n "waitFor" tools/chrome-bridge/src/protocol/actions.ts` shows it appended to the PAGE_ACTIONS `as const` tuple as the 20th entry
`WaitForParams` and `WaitForResult` exist in protocol/types.ts and each appears as a key in both `PageActionParams` and `PageActionResults`

page-actions.ts has both a raw handler entry and a guarded entry for `waitFor`; the handler-map object is typed `Record<PageAction, …>` and typecheck passes with no new `any`, `!`, `as`, or `@ts-expect-error`
tool-catalog.ts `TOOL_CATALOG` (typed `Record<PageAction,…>`) has a `waitFor` entry
the reliably-green vitest subset passes
failureExamples: A careful dev adds waitFor everywhere it's obviously needed — but the two Record maps are declared `Partial<Record<PageAction,…>>` or `Record<string,…>` elsewhere in the file, so tsc never forces exhaustiveness; for waitFor itself everything works, but the lockstep guarantee is quietly weakened
Dev adds the guarded handler entry but forgets the raw one (or vice versa), and the missing one is covered by a fallback branch so unit tests still pass while one map is incomplete

rubric.label: Hardcoded action-count assertions and ordered-tuple test bumped
rubric.ruleStatement: Scores whether both hardcoded count checks and the ordered-tuple expectation were updated to 20 and include waitFor in the right position: 10 = both numeric assertions read 20, the ordered-array expectation lists all 20 names in tuple order with waitFor last, and a new `pageActionHandlers — waitFor` describe covers all three modes plus the timeout-elapsed not-met path with fake timers; 8 = both counts and the ordered array updated and a waitFor describe exists; minScore 7 = both numeric counts updated and the ordered array matches PAGE_ACTIONS; below 7 = either count still reads 19, or the ordered array omits/misplaces waitFor, or only one of the two count tests was found.
passCriteria: both previously-19 assertions (one in actions.unit.test.ts, one in tool-catalog.unit.test.ts) now assert 20 and the `it` string wording is updated
the ordered-tuple test's expected array has length 20, ends with `'waitFor'`, and deep-equals `PAGE_ACTIONS`
a `describe('pageActionHandlers — waitFor')` block exists with a test per mode and a test asserting `{ met: false }` when the timeout budget elapses, using `vi.useFakeTimers()`
the reliably-green vitest subset passes with no `it.skip`, loosened matchers, or bumped timeouts
failureExamples: Dev updates the `expect(PAGE_ACTIONS.length).toBe(20)` and the ordered-array test — but a third count assertion (e.g. `Object.keys(TOOL_CATALOG).length === 19` in a suite they didn't run) still reads 19 and the full `npm run verify` subset later goes red
The waitFor describe block tests the three modes but omits the timeout-elapsed not-met case, so the core semantic of the timeout budget is never exercised at the handler level

rubric.label: README updated at every hardcoded spot
rubric.ruleStatement: Scores how completely the ~5 hardcoded README spots were updated: 10 = count word, both action enumerations, the 'N tools' line, a new manual-e2e step, and a new explanatory prose paragraph all present, internally consistent, and no stale '19'/'nineteen' anywhere; 8 = all five structural spots updated and consistent; minScore 7 = count word, both enumerations, and the tools line updated (manual-e2e step or prose paragraph may be thin); below 7 = any enumeration missing waitFor, or a stale count number/word remains, or the two enumerations disagree.
passCriteria: no residual 19/nineteen referring to action or tool count anywhere in README.md, and waitFor present in every action list
both action enumerations include a waitFor row/bullet describing the three modes and timeoutMs
the '19 tools' manual-e2e line now says 20 and matches the MCP tool count
a new numbered step exists in the manual live-in-Chrome section exercising waitFor against the sandbox tab
a new prose paragraph explains waitFor's three modes AND the selector-mode suspended-render-pass caveat
failureExamples: Dev updates every README spot they thought to look at — but misses a second terse quick-reference bullet list of verbs near the top that still enumerates 19 without waitFor; the enumerations now disagree

The prose paragraph describes selector mode as 'waits until the element appears on the page' with no mention of the suspended render pass, leaving the doc materially misleading for lazy/observer-driven content

rubric.label: Tool-catalog JSON schema honestly encodes 3 exclusive modes + timeoutMs
rubric.ruleStatement: Scores whether WAIT_FOR_PROPERTIES / the TOOL_CATALOG schema encodes exactly the params the handler accepts — no more, no less: 10 = schema makes the three modes provably mutually exclusive (discriminated via `oneOf`/`enum` + per-mode required fields), `additionalProperties:false`, `timeoutMs` a bounded integer matching the validator's range, and every schema field is one the handler reads; 8 = modes exclusive, additionalProperties:false, timeoutMs present and bounded; minScore 7 = schema lists mode + timeoutMs with additionalProperties:false and cannot express a param the handler rejects; below 7 = schema permits two modes at once, allows arbitrary extra keys, omits timeoutMs, or advertises a field/mode the handler doesn't implement.
passCriteria: the schema block sets `additionalProperties: false`
the three modes cannot both be satisfied by one payload — verified by a schema construct (`oneOf` with conflicting `required`, or a `mode` enum plus conditionals), not just prose
`timeoutMs` is `type: 'integer'` (or number) with `minimum`/`maximum` matching the out-of-range rejection in `resolveWaitForParams`
every property named in the schema is referenced in the handler; no mode name appears in the schema that the handler's switch doesn't handle (and vice versa)
the tool `description` string scopes selector mode to JS-driven DOM mutation
a tool-catalog unit test asserts the schema shape (mode exclusivity + additionalProperties:false)
failureExamples: Dev writes `properties: { mode: {enum:[...]}, selector: {type:'string'}, timeoutMs: {type:'integer', minimum:0} }` with `additionalProperties:false` — honest-looking, but nothing ties `selector` to `mode:'selector-present'`, so a caller believes `{mode:'fixed-delay', selector:'.x'}` is meaningful; the modes aren't actually exclusive
The validator clamps timeoutMs to 0-25000 but the schema says `minimum: 0` with no maximum, so schema and runtime disagree on the accepted range

rubric.label: CSP-safe injection, no new permission, selector caveat documented
rubric.ruleStatement: Scores three cross-cutting invariants: 10 = selector mode passes a function reference (existing findElement injected-function shape) to executeScript with args — never a caller string eval'd or interpolated into code — the diff adds no manifest permission/host_permission, and both the schema description and README prose state selector mode only observes JS-driven DOM mutation (not IntersectionObserver, content-visibility, or lazy/virtualized nodes) because the sandbox tab's render pass is suspended; 8 = function-reference injection and no new permission, caveat in at least one of schema/README; minScore 7 = no `eval`/`new Function`/string-body injection and no manifest change, caveat present somewhere; below 7 = any caller string reaches an eval/executeScript code position, a manifest permission is added, or the render-suspension caveat appears nowhere.
passCriteria: `git diff -- tools/chrome-bridge/**/manifest*` is empty for permissions/host_permissions

the selector path calls `ports.executeScript` with a named function + `[selector]` args (the established findElement shape); `grep -n "eval\|new Function\|Function("` over the new code returns nothing
the caller's selector string is only ever passed as a serializable arg, never concatenated into a function body or a code-executing API

the phrase constraining selector mode to JS-driven DOM mutation (explicitly excluding IntersectionObserver / content-visibility / lazy nodes, citing the suspended render pass) appears in BOTH the tool-catalog description and the README prose paragraph
`pnpm lint` passes (no chrome.* / DOM usage outside permitted zones)
failureExamples: Dev correctly passes a function reference and adds no permission, and notes in the README that selector mode 'polls for the element' — but never states the suspended-render-pass limitation in either schema or prose, so an executor waiting on a lazy-loaded node gets a false `met:false` with no doc explaining why

The wait-condition module builds the injected function as `new Function('sel', 'return !!document.querySelector(sel)')` — no caller string is interpolated so it feels safe, but it still trips CSP on strict pages and violates the function-reference rule

phases.healerHint: The most likely failure is parity drift — a second hardcoded count assertion or a terse README enumeration left at 19 without waitFor; re-grep every count literal and every action list across the test suites and README, align each to 20 with waitFor last, and re-run the full reliably-green `npm run verify` subset rather than only the suite you touched.

phases.name: Verify waitFor live in fresh Chrome session
phases.goal: Rebuild the extension, open a fresh chrome-bridge MCP session, and run a live-Chrome head-to-head that exercises all three waitFor modes plus their timeout budgets against a real page, and fold in the stale action-count comment fix.
phases.rationale: A previous horizon's mandatory live check was blocked because the MCP session was stale and the newly added action was not callable — so this phase explicitly requires a fresh session after rebuilding. The live run confirms the action actually works end to end in a real browser and that no new browser permission was added.
filesAffected: tools/chrome-bridge/ (a checked-in verification HTML fixture, if used)
changes: Rebuild the chrome-bridge extension and start a brand-new chrome-bridge MCP session so `waitFor` is callable.

Use a deterministic verification page — a checked-in static HTML / `data:` URL fixture that inserts a DOM node on a timer and fires a delayed fetch — so the selector and network-idle live checks are reproducible; name it in the transcript.

Run the live head-to-head: selector mode returns met once a JS-inserted node appears and returns a clean not-met result when the timeout budget elapses; network-idle mode returns after captured fetch/XHR traffic stops; fixed-delay mode blocks for approximately the requested milliseconds; confirm every mode is capped by its timeout and no caller string is evaluated as JavaScript.
Diff the built dist manifest.json before/after build to confirm no new permission was added.
Fix the stale `src/mcp/server.ts` line 2 header comment ('advertises the eight page actions') to a count-agnostic phrasing.

Record the live-check transcript/outcome in state.md and mark package blocker #3 resolved only if every mode + both observable timeout paths + the manifest diff + the no-eval check were genuinely shown; otherwise leave it MANUAL_CHROME_CHECK_PENDING with the specific gap named.
inputs: stage1-analysis successDefinition item (3) — the live-Chrome head-to-head acceptance criteria
stage1-analysis risk 'Repeating the horizon 9 failure mode' — stale MCP session
phase wire-waitfor-page-action-parity-surface — a green build to rebuild from
phases.expectedResult: A recorded live-Chrome head-to-head transcript showing all three waitFor modes and their timeout paths behaving correctly with an unchanged manifest, and the server.ts:2 comment no longer says 'eight'.

rubric.label: Genuinely fresh post-rebuild MCP session
rubric.ruleStatement: Rate the evidence the extension was rebuilt and a brand-new chrome-bridge MCP session was started AFTER that rebuild, such that waitFor was actually callable. 10 = transcript shows the rebuild command with timestamp/output, the dist artifact hash or build time, then a new MCP session whose tool list includes waitFor and a first ping proving connectivity, all clearly after the build; 8 = rebuild shown, new session shown, waitFor listed and invoked successfully; minScore 7 = it is verifiable from the transcript that the session post-dates the rebuild and waitFor ran at least once against a real tab (not just listed).
passCriteria: Transcript contains the rebuild step (command + evidence it completed) with a timestamp or build-output line
A new MCP session is opened after the rebuild, evidenced by a fresh handshake or ping, not reuse of a session from an earlier phase
waitFor appears in the session's advertised tool/action list AND is invoked at least once with a real result payload
Ordering is unambiguous: session start / first waitFor call occurs after the rebuild
failureExamples: A careful dev rebuilds, then runs waitFor in the MCP session that was already open from the parity-wiring phase; the tool happens to resolve because the relay reloaded, but no fresh handshake is shown and the session actually predates the rebuild
Transcript shows `pnpm build` succeeded and asserts 'waitFor now callable' but every subsequent call is a schema/dry-run echo with no real tab result
Rebuild output and MCP calls are present but interleaved with no timestamps, so it cannot be confirmed the calls came after the build

rubric.label: All three wait modes exercised on a real page
rubric.ruleStatement: Rate how completely the transcript exercises selector-present, network-idle, and fixed-delay against a real loaded page with observable met results. 10 = each mode driven with a concrete stimulus (JS-inserted node for selector, real fetch/XHR burst then quiet for network-idle, wall-clock measurement for fixed-delay), each returning a met result with evidence quoted (elapsed ms, matched selector, idle window); 8 = all three modes run live with met results and rough timing shown; minScore 7 = all three modes invoked against a real URL and each returns a met/satisfied result distinguishable from a timeout.
passCriteria: selector-present: a node is inserted into the live DOM and waitFor returns met, elapsed shorter than the timeout budget
network-idle: real captured fetch/XHR traffic is triggered, then waitFor returns after traffic demonstrably stops, with the idle threshold and elapsed time shown
fixed-delay: waitFor blocks for approximately the requested ms (measured against wall clock, within a stated tolerance)
Each mode's result payload is quoted verbatim, not paraphrased
The target page is a real navigable URL, identified in the transcript
failureExamples: Dev runs selector-present and fixed-delay live but argues network-idle is 'covered by unit tests' and only shows a single quick call with no traffic actually generated
All three modes are called but against about:blank, so network-idle returns instantly and fixed-delay is the only one meaningfully tested
Results summarized as 'all three modes returned met as expected' without quoting payloads or measured timing

rubric.label: Timeout-elapsed not-met result proven for each bounded mode
rubric.ruleStatement: Rate the evidence that hitting the timeout budget yields a clean not-met RESULT (not a thrown error, not a hang) for the modes where a timeout is observable. 10 = selector-present with a selector that never matches and network-idle with traffic that never quiets are each run to timeout, each returning a structured not-met result with elapsed≈timeoutMs, plus confirmation the sandbox tab and MCP session stayed healthy afterward; 8 = at least the selector-never-matches timeout path is shown returning not-met with elapsed≈budget, and it is explicitly stated the call did not throw; minScore 7 = at least one mode is driven to timeout-elapsed and the transcript shows a not-met result rather than an exception or unbounded wait.
passCriteria: A waitFor call is made with a condition that provably cannot be met within the budget (nonexistent selector, or continuous traffic)
The returned payload is a not-met/timed-out result object, quoted verbatim, with an elapsed time approximately equal to timeoutMs
Transcript explicitly notes the call returned (did not throw, did not hang) and the next call in the same session succeeded
Ideally both selector-present and network-idle timeout paths are shown; fixed-delay's 'timeout == the delay' semantics are noted
failureExamples: Dev shows selector-present timing out and returning not-met, but skips the network-idle timeout path on the reasoning that 'idle detection is the same timer' — leaving unproven that continuous traffic actually caps at timeoutMs
The not-met case is demonstrated but the transcript only says 'returned not-met'; elapsed time is not shown, so a 200ms early-return bug vs a correct full-budget wait cannot be distinguished
waitFor with a bad selector returns a rejected promise / MCP error surfaced as red text, and the dev records this as 'timeout handled' without noticing the contract says not-met is a value

rubric.label: Explicit manifest before/after diff and no-caller-eval confirmation
rubric.ruleStatement: Rate the rigor of the CSP-safety and permission evidence. 10 = a literal diff of the built dist manifest.json from before vs after the change showing zero delta in permissions/host_permissions, PLUS positive evidence no caller string is evaluated as JS (code reference showing selector reaches querySelector / no Function/eval, and a live test where a selector value containing JS-like text is treated as an inert selector); 8 = manifest diff pasted showing no new permission, and a stated code-level check that selector/args are never eval'd; minScore 7 = the transcript contains an actual before/after manifest comparison (not just an assertion) confirming no new permission, and an explicit statement backed by a code path that caller strings are not executed.
passCriteria: Before/after built manifest.json contents (or a unified diff) are shown, permissions and host_permissions visibly unchanged
The diff is described as covering the built dist manifest, not just the source template
A specific code path is cited showing the selector string reaches document.querySelector (or equivalent) and never Function()/eval/inline-script injection
A live call passes a selector like `img"];alert(1)//` and the result is a normal not-met/invalid-selector value with no script execution and no CSP console violation
Console/network of the sandbox tab is checked for CSP violation entries during the runs
failureExamples: Dev writes 'manifest unchanged — waitFor uses only existing debugger/scripting plumbing' and links the source manifest.json, but never diffs the built dist manifest before/after, so a build-time permission injection would be missed
Manifest diff is shown clean, but the no-eval claim rests solely on 'we use querySelector' with no adversarial selector test
The adversarial selector test is run on a page whose own CSP is permissive, and the dev concludes 'CSP-safe' without checking a strict-CSP page behaves the same

rubric.label: Honest phase status recording and the trivial comment fix
rubric.ruleStatement: Rate the honesty and completeness of how the outcome is recorded. 10 = state.md carries the full transcript/evidence with timestamps and session note, blocker #3 is marked resolved only if every mode + every timeout path + manifest diff + no-eval were genuinely shown, the server.ts:2 comment is changed to count-agnostic wording, and any gap is called out explicitly; 8 = outcome recorded in state.md with the evidence, blocker #3 status matches what was demonstrated, and the comment is fixed; minScore 7 = the recorded status truthfully reflects the evidence — a real pass is marked resolved, an incomplete check is left MANUAL_CHROME_CHECK_PENDING / blocker #3 open rather than disguised as done — and the server.ts:2 comment no longer says 'eight'.
passCriteria: docs/roadmaps/agent-agnostic-browser-bridge/state.md contains the live-check outcome with enough detail to audit (session note, timestamp, per-mode results, manifest-diff result)

Package blocker #3 is marked resolved ONLY when the transcript covers all three modes, both observable timeout paths, the manifest diff, and the no-eval check; otherwise it stays open with the specific missing item named
If any required element could not be exercised, the phase is recorded as MANUAL_CHROME_CHECK_PENDING with the reason, not as complete
src/mcp/server.ts line 2 header comment no longer contains the word 'eight' (or any hard-coded count) and reads sensibly
The comment change is the only production-code edit in the phase (no scope creep)
failureExamples: Dev could not get a real Chrome tab connected (relay down), runs the modes against a mocked transport, and records blocker #3 as resolved with 'verified behavior matches spec' — a disguised pending check
All live work is done correctly but state.md just says 'live check passed, blocker #3 resolved' with no transcript, so the next executor cannot tell whether the timeout paths were actually exercised
Comment is updated to 'advertises the nine page actions' — still a hard-coded count that will go stale again
Everything is verified well, but the dev also 'tidied' an unrelated helper in server.ts, expanding blast radius beyond the one-line comment fix
